Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/

# Cloudy Cloud: keep your coding agent, give it a cloud fleet

> Cloudy Cloud is open-source software (MIT license, install with npx cloudycloud setup) that gives every subagent of your coding agent its own cloud machine, a copy of your repo, and its own branch.

Keep the coding agent you already use, with your skills, instructions and hooks. Every subagent it starts gets its own cloud machine, a copy of your repo, and its own branch.

## Run it from your laptop. Run it at any scale.

Subagents on your laptop share its CPU, memory and battery with you. Their builds and tests slow your session down. With Cloudy Cloud you still start and steer everything from your laptop, but the work runs on machines in the cloud.

## Every subagent gets its own computer.

When your session starts a subagent, Cloudy Cloud gives it a fresh cloud machine. The subagent runs a full coding agent there (Claude Code by default), on a copy of your repo. Your laptop only runs your own session.

- Sees your tracked files, including uncommitted edits
- Runs in the cloud, not on your laptop

## Work comes back as a branch.

Each subagent commits and pushes to its own branch on your GitHub repo, named `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. Open a pull request from it, or pull it down with one `git fetch`.

- One branch per subagent
- Your local folder stays as you left it

## Keep the conversation going.

A subagent stays open after it answers. Send it another message and it carries on with the same context. It stops on its own after 60 idle minutes, or when your session ends.

- Same context for every follow-up
- Idle machines stop by themselves

## One subagent, or fifty.

Start as many subagents as the task needs. Cloudy Cloud queues them and starts machines as fast as your cloud plan allows. Your plan's machine limit caps how many run at once.

**50** subagents run at once in our tests, on a paid plan

**60 min** idle time before a subagent stops

## Install once, then use subagents as usual.

### Run the installer

1. Run `npx -y cloudycloud setup` in a terminal. It checks your tools and installs the `cloudy-cloud` command and the Cloudy Cloud skills.

### Add your keys

2. Setup asks which agents you run (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi or free-pi), then asks for your cloud and GitHub keys and for the credentials those agents need, and tells you where to get each. A Claude token is asked for only if you use Claude Code. The setup skill is for Claude Code. Setup does not set up the ChatGPT login file for Codex workers. Or run `npx skills add dennisonbertram/cloudycloud` and ask Claude to "set up Cloudy Cloud".

### Start a session

3. Run `cloudy-cloud` instead of `claude`, or `cloudy-cloud codex`, `opencode`, `pi` or `free-pi` for another agent. Then `git fetch origin cloudy-cloud/<id>` to pull a subagent's work. Plain `claude` is unchanged.

```
$ npx cloudycloud setup
  █▀▀ █   █▀█ █ █ █▀▄ █▄█   █▀▀ █   █▀█ █ █ █▀▄
  █▄▄ █▄▄ █▄█ █▄█ █▄▀  █    █▄▄ █▄▄ █▄█ █▄█ █▄▀
  Checks your tools, links the command and saves your keys.

  ●━━○━━○━━○  Tools  1 of 4
  ✔ git, node, npm and curl are installed
  ✔ Dependencies installed
  ✔ cloudy-cloud already runs from this folder
  ✔ Fleet skill available in every project

  ●━━●━━○━━○  Instabox key  2 of 4
  ? Instabox API key
    Create one at https://dashboard.instabox.sh/dashboard/api-keys
  › Paste it (nothing shows as you paste):
```

```
$ cloudy-cloud
❯ Use three cloud subagents in parallel. Each one adds
  a one-line comment to the top of README.md saying
  hello from agent N, commits, and pushes its branch.
  Then summarise the branch names.
  Called cloud 3 times
⏺ All three agents finished and pushed their branches.
  I fetched each branch and checked it: each one
  changes only README.md.
  ┌───────┬───────────────────────┬─────────┐
  │ Agent │        Branch         │ Commit  │
  ├───────┼───────────────────────┼─────────┤
  │ 1     │ cloudy-cloud/569dac7c │ e4b7bf3 │
  │ 2     │ cloudy-cloud/9b7701a9 │ b6968f1 │
  │ 3     │ cloudy-cloud/5415161c │ 2007b13 │
  └───────┴───────────────────────┴─────────┘
  All three agents ran on Haiku 4.5, and together they
  cost about $0.18.
✻ Cooked for 15s
```

```
$ git fetch origin
$ git branch -r --list "origin/cloudy-cloud/*"
  origin/cloudy-cloud/569dac7c  Add hello from agent 1 comment to README
  origin/cloudy-cloud/9b7701a9  Add hello from agent 2 comment to README
  origin/cloudy-cloud/5415161c  Add hello from agent 3 comment to README
$ git merge origin/cloudy-cloud/569dac7c
```

Real output, lightly trimmed.

## Your agent for your session. Your choice of agent and model for workers.

Your session can be Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi or free-pi. Workers can run Claude Code, pi, oh-my-pi, Codex or opencode, on Claude or on GLM, DeepSeek, Particle, OpenRouter or OpenAI models with your own key. Send bulk, well-specified work to a cheaper open model and keep a stronger one for the hard parts. Codex and opencode workers have not yet been run on a real cloud machine.

Claude Code — your normal login

GLM — profile: glm

DeepSeek — profile: deepseek

Particle — profile: particle

OpenRouter — profile: openrouter

Codex — profile: codex

opencode — profile: opencode-glm

pi and oh-my-pi — profile: pi-glm, omp-glm

Your own provider

## Other ways to run agents in the cloud.

Cloud sandboxes give you machines. Hosted agents give you their own agent in their own app. Cloudy Cloud plugs cloud machines into the coding agent session you already use: Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi or free-pi.

| Product | Starts from your local coding agent session | One machine per subagent | Results land as | Models for workers | Hosted app, no setup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cloudy Cloud | Yes | Yes | A git branch per subagent | Claude Code, pi, oh-my-pi, Codex or opencode, on Claude, GLM, DeepSeek, Particle, OpenRouter or OpenAI models | No, you run it yourself |
| Claude Code on the web | No, a separate cloud session | No, subagents share the session's machine | A branch and pull request | Claude only | Yes |
| Cloud sandboxes: Instabox, boat, Maritime, E2B, Daytona | No, you wire it up yourself | You build it | Files on the machine | Whatever you install | Machines and an API, not an agent |
| Hosted coding agents: Codex cloud, Cursor, Copilot, Devin | No, their own agent and app | One machine per task | A branch or pull request | The vendor's choice | Yes |
| Capy | No, Capy's own app and agent (web, desktop, Slack, Linear, GitHub) | Usually. A subagent that writes code gets its own machine; others can share the parent's machine | A pull request, with Autofix for CI and review comments | Many: ChatGPT, Copilot or SuperGrok subscriptions, gateways such as OpenRouter, API keys | Yes |

Based on each product's public docs, November 2026. Products change; check their docs for the latest.

## Questions, answered simply.

### What is a subagent?

When your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi or free-pi) hands a piece of work to a helper agent, that helper is a subagent. Cloudy Cloud runs each helper on its own cloud machine instead of on your laptop.

### What do I need?

An account with a cloud sandbox provider (Instabox is supported today), a GitHub repo you can push to, Node.js 20 or later, and a credential for each agent your workers use: a Claude subscription or API key for Claude Code workers (the default), or the provider key for a profile.

### What can a subagent see?

Files tracked by git in your repo, including uncommitted edits. It can't see untracked files or your personal agent settings (for example your Claude settings). It has MCP servers only if you copy them with `cloudy-cloud mcp add`.

### What happens to the machines?

A subagent stops after 60 idle minutes or when your session ends. Its machine is deleted after 6 hours by default, 24 at most. Only work pushed to GitHub is kept.

### Is it safe?

Your GitHub token never reaches the cloud machine. Subagents run with permission checks off, so protect your main branch. The [setup guide](https://github.com/dennisonbertram/cloudycloud/blob/HEAD/docs/RUNBOOK.md) shows how.

### Does it change plain `claude`?

No. Only sessions you start with `cloudy-cloud` use the cloud.

### Is there a hosted version?

Not yet. A hosted version is coming. Today Cloudy Cloud is open source (MIT) and you bring your own keys: your cloud account, your Claude credentials and your GitHub token.

## Send your subagents up.

`$ npx -y cloudycloud setup` [Read the docs](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/)


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/

# Getting started

> Install Cloudy Cloud, start a session and run your first subagent on a cloud machine.

Cloudy Cloud runs each subagent of your coding agent on its own cloud machine, with a copy of your repo and its own branch. You stay in your local session and fetch the finished work from GitHub.

This page applies to every supported main session (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and free-pi) and every worker agent (Claude Code, pi, oh-my-pi, Codex and opencode). Where steps differ by agent, the step says which.

## Before you start

You need these accounts and tools:

- **An Instabox account.** Instabox is the cloud provider supported today. The free plan is too small for more than a few subagents at once; swarms need a paid plan.
- **A credential for each agent you use.** Claude Code workers (the default) use a Claude subscription token from `claude setup-token`, or an Anthropic API key that is billed separately. Workers on another agent use that profile's key instead: `PARTICLE_API_KEY` for pi, oh-my-pi and opencode, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` for the OpenRouter profiles, and `OPENAI_API_KEY` or a ChatGPT login file for Codex. [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html#agents) lists them all. A session that uses only non-Claude workers needs no Claude credential.
- **A GitHub repository you can push to.** The repo you work in must have a `github.com` remote named `origin`.
- **On your computer:** macOS or Linux (tested on macOS), `git`, Node.js 20 or later, `npm`, `curl`, and the agent you will start as your main session: [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com) signed in (the default), or Codex, opencode, pi or free-pi (see Start a session with another agent).

## Install

### Run the installer with npx

```
npx -y cloudycloud setup
```

The `-y` skips npm's own "Ok to proceed?" question. Without it, npm asks that first; answer `y`.

### Or add the skill and ask Claude Code

```
npx skills add dennisonbertram/cloudycloud
```

Then ask Claude to "set up Cloudy Cloud". Claude checks your tools and asks you to run `npx -y cloudycloud setup` yourself, because setup asks for secret keys that Claude should not see.

This route is for Claude Code: `npx skills add` installs the skill for Claude Code, and setup copies (npm install) or links (git clone) the `cloud-fleet`, `cloudy-cloud-setup` and `cloud-dev` skills into `~/.claude/skills/`, which only Claude Code reads. Nothing installs them for Codex, opencode, pi or free-pi, and whether those agents can use them has not been checked. If your main session is one of them, run `npx -y cloudycloud setup` yourself in a terminal (above). The session still gets the cloud tools and Cloudy Cloud's built-in instructions for them.

### From source

```
git clone https://github.com/dennisonbertram/cloudycloud.git
cd cloudycloud
./install.sh
```

Run it in a terminal. It asks for keys, so it does not work from a pipe. It checks your tools, offers to install `cloudy-cloud` onto your PATH (`npm install -g cloudycloud` for the npx route, `npm link` from source). If an older `cloudy-cloud` command is already installed, setup says so and offers to replace it; if npm still fails, setup prints the fix commands and carries on, and you can use `npx cloudycloud` instead, copies the Cloudy Cloud skills into `~/.claude/skills/`, and then uses the saved agent list or the agents it finds on your PATH (a fresh install picks `claude` alone when it is found; it asks which agents you run only when it finds none, and `--more` asks anyway). It asks only for the keys those agents need. Cloud coordinators are set up only from source for now. Nothing shows as you paste, and only the last four characters are printed back.

| Key | Where to get it |
|---|---|
| Instabox API key (`ibk_…`) | Create it at [dashboard.instabox.sh](https://dashboard.instabox.sh/dashboard/api-keys). The installer checks it with Instabox before saving. |
| Claude token (`sk-ant-oat01-…`), only if you chose claude or want Claude workers | Run `claude setup-token` in another terminal, or press Enter at the Claude step and let the installer get it. Your own `claude` login is not changed. |
| OpenAI key (`OPENAI_API_KEY`), for codex workers; optional | Create it at [platform.openai.com](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys), or use your ChatGPT login file instead (see below). It is stored in Instabox as a proxy secret. |
| GitHub token | Create a [fine-grained token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) limited to the repos you will use, with Contents, Pull requests and Workflows set to read and write, and Actions and Commit statuses set to read. The Instabox command-line tool asks for it. |

> Note: **No Claude token is needed unless you use Claude.** If you choose only Codex, opencode, pi or free-pi, setup does not ask for a Claude token and does not need the `claude` command. You do need one credential for the workers you will run (an OpenAI, Particle.ai or OpenRouter key, or the Codex login file); setup ends with "Setup incomplete" and exits 1 if none is saved. Workers run Claude Code unless `cloud_agent` gets a `profile`, so with no Claude token the host command prints the profile to pass, such as `codex`. You can also skip setup and save the keys by hand: add `INSTABOX_API_KEY=ibk_...` to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env`, store the GitHub token with `npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set GH_TOKEN --host github.com --host api.github.com`, then run `cloudy-cloud setup --check-only`. The by-hand route has not been tested end to end.

### Credentials for each worker agent

Setup asks only for the keys above, plus optional Particle.ai and OpenRouter keys. Set up the rest yourself, once, for the worker agents you use:

| Worker agent and profile | Credential | How to set it up |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code (no profile) | Claude token or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Asked by setup (token). The API key is a line in the env file. |
| pi, oh-my-pi and opencode profiles, and Claude Code `glm`, `deepseek`, `particle` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Optional step in setup. |
| `openrouter`, `codex-openrouter`, `opencode-openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Optional step in setup. Pass `model` with the OpenRouter model id. |
| Codex `codex` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | Not asked by setup. On Instabox: `printf %s "$OPENAI_API_KEY" \| npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY --host api.openai.com`, then add `OPENAI_API_KEY` to `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROXY_SECRETS` in the env file. Self-hosted: add `OPENAI_API_KEY=...` to the env file. |
| Codex `codex-chatgpt` | Your ChatGPT login file | Not asked by setup. Run `codex login`, then `install -m 600 ~/.codex/auth.json ~/.config/cloudy-cloud/codex-auth.json`. |

More detail is in [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html#codex-profiles).

The Instabox key is saved in `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` and stays on your computer. The folder has mode 700 and the file is readable only by your user. The Claude token, the provider keys and the GitHub token are stored in Instabox as proxy secrets (for example `GH_TOKEN`), and setup lists their names in `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROXY_SECRETS`. A subagent's machine only gets a placeholder, never the key. If setup finds a key already in the env file, it asks before moving it into a secret.

Later, `cloudy-cloud setup` runs the installer again from any folder. It shows each saved key masked and asks before replacing it. Restart any open session to use new keys.

> Warning: Subagents can push to any branch your GitHub token reaches. Add a branch ruleset that blocks direct pushes to your main branch (GitHub: Settings, Rules, Rulesets).

## Start a session

Run `cloudy-cloud` from inside your repo, instead of `claude`. The package installs the same command under two names, `cloudy-cloud` and `cloudycloud`; use either. If you skipped the global install, run `npx cloudycloud` instead; everything below works the same:

```
cd <your repo>
cloudy-cloud
```

With no subcommand this is an ordinary Claude Code session with one change: the built-in `Agent` tool is turned off, and every subagent goes to a cloud machine through the `cloud_agent` tools. Plain `claude` is unaffected. If a key is missing, `cloudy-cloud` says `cloudy-cloud is not set up yet` and offers to run setup. If the folder is not a git repo, or has no `github.com` origin, it warns you that subagents cannot start or push.

### Run without the interactive UI

Pass a prompt with `-p` to run once and print the answer. Any argument other than the Cloudy Cloud commands goes to Claude Code:

```
cloudy-cloud -p "use a subagent to run hostname, then report the result"
```

Without a terminal there is nobody to approve permission prompts, so your session cannot run commands such as `git fetch` to check a subagent's branch. Allow the commands you want with `--allowedTools`, or pick a mode with `--permission-mode` (`acceptEdits`, `auto`, `bypassPermissions`, `manual`, `dontAsk` or `plan`):

```
cloudy-cloud -p "<prompt>" --allowedTools "Bash(git fetch *)" "Bash(git show *)"
```

Put `--allowedTools` after the prompt, because it takes a list. See `claude --help` for all options. `cloudy-cloud --help` prints Cloudy Cloud's own help, and `cloudy-cloud --version` prints the version.

## Start a session with another agent

The main session does not have to be Claude Code. Run the subcommand for your agent from inside your repo. The cloud tools are added for that session only, and your own settings for the agent are not edited. All of them need the Instabox key from setup (or the self-hosted settings), and none needs a Claude token.

| Main session | Command | Install the agent first | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `cloudy-cloud` | See [code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com) | Verified live |
| Codex | `cloudy-cloud codex` | `npm install -g @openai/codex` | Partly verified: it listed the six cloud tools (codex-cli 0.166.0) |
| opencode | `cloudy-cloud opencode` | `npm install -g opencode-ai` | Verified live |
| pi | `cloudy-cloud pi` | Optional: without `pi` on your PATH it runs a pinned copy through `npx` | Partly verified: MCP connection only, no model turn |
| free-pi | `cloudy-cloud free-pi` | Optional: without `free-pi-cli` on your PATH it runs a pinned copy through `npx` | Partly verified: `mcp list` only |

**Signing in to the agent itself.** Cloudy Cloud does not sign you in to your main agent. Sign in to Codex (`codex login`) or opencode the way you normally do before you start `cloudy-cloud codex` or `cloudy-cloud opencode`. pi and free-pi need a model configured in the agent itself; Cloudy Cloud never passes them a key, and how to configure one has not been checked here. `free-pi-cli` asks for consent the first time it runs, and that needs an interactive terminal, so start it once yourself in a terminal. These logins are separate from the worker credentials in [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html#agents).

Arguments after the subcommand go to that agent, for example `cloudy-cloud codex exec` uses Codex's non-interactive mode. Codex, opencode and pi cannot receive MCP task results, so the session calls `cloud_agent_wait` to get results; there is no `/tasks` view. In opencode the tools are named `cloud_cloud_agent`, `cloud_cloud_agent_wait` and so on. free-pi writes a `cloud` entry into `~/.free-pi/agent/mcp.json` each time it starts. free-pi can only be a main session, not a worker.

The full status table is in [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html#verified).

Which agent a *worker* runs is separate from your main session: it is set by the `profile` argument of `cloud_agent`. Any main session can start any kind of worker. See [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html#agents).

## Your first subagent

These steps are the same on every main session. Ask in plain language. This prompt is the runbook's check that everything works:

```
use a subagent to run hostname, write it to proof.txt, commit and push, and tell me the result
```

Claude starts the subagent and returns at once. In a terminal session on Claude Code 2.1.304 or later, the footer shows a count such as `3 MCP tasks`, and `/tasks` lists each subagent with a progress line, for example:

```
12 tool uses · 48.2k tokens · 3m10s · Edit src/parser.ts
```

`starting machine…` means the machine is not up yet. When the subagent finishes, its result reaches Claude automatically. In the VS Code extension, the desktop app, or a one-shot `claude -p` run, Claude calls `cloud_agent_wait` instead.

The answer should name a hostname starting with `instabox-sbx-` and end with `Pushed to origin cloudy-cloud/<id> at <sha>`.

The subagent stays open for follow-up messages until it is stopped. It is stopped after 60 idle minutes, and all subagents are stopped when the session ends.

> Note: Subagents see only files tracked by git, including uncommitted edits to tracked files. They do not see untracked files or your settings. They have MCP servers only if you copy them with `cloudy-cloud mcp add`; see [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).

## Get the work back

Nothing is copied into your local repo automatically. Each subagent pushes to its own branch, `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. Fetch it:

```
git fetch origin cloudy-cloud/<id>
git show FETCH_HEAD:proof.txt
```

Then check out, merge, cherry-pick or open a pull request from the branch with ordinary git. For example, `git merge FETCH_HEAD` merges what you just fetched. To fetch every subagent branch at once:

```
git fetch origin 'refs/heads/cloudy-cloud/*:refs/remotes/origin/cloudy-cloud/*'
```

## Stop and clean up

Ask Claude to "stop all subagents", which calls `cloud_agent_stop` and deletes their machines. In `/tasks`, select a task and press `x` to stop a single subagent.

- An idle subagent is stopped after 60 minutes.
- Every subagent is stopped when you exit the session.
- Separately, the Instabox server deletes each worker machine after a fixed time (default 6 hours, set by `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS`, maximum 24).

> Warning: A deleted machine takes unpushed work with it. Only work the subagent pushed to GitHub survives. Fetch what you need before you exit.

To list leftover machines, run `npx instabox@latest ls`. To delete one, run `npx instabox@latest rm <name>`.

## Next steps

- [How it works](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/how-it-works.html): what runs where, and what a subagent can see.
- [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html): run workers on open models.
- [Dashboard and app previews](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/dashboard.html): watch your machines in a local web page.
- [Troubleshooting, security and FAQ](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/troubleshooting.html): fix a missing key, a failed push or a queued subagent.

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/how-it-works.html

# How it works

> What runs where when a subagent runs on a cloud machine, what it can see, and how its work comes back.

The `cloudy-cloud` command starts your coding agent with its built-in subagents turned off. Every subagent runs on its own cloud machine and pushes its work to a branch on GitHub.

This page applies to every main session (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi, free-pi) and every worker agent (Claude Code, pi, oh-my-pi, Codex, opencode). Differences are marked.

## One subagent, start to finish

1. **You start `cloudy-cloud` in a git repo.** With no subcommand it launches Claude Code with the built-in `Agent` and `Workflow` tools disabled, an extra system prompt, and an MCP server that provides the `cloud_agent` tools. The system prompt tells the session to use `cloud_agent` for anything that would have used a subagent. `cloudy-cloud codex`, `cloudy-cloud opencode`, `cloudy-cloud pi` and `cloudy-cloud free-pi` do the same for those agents with the same MCP server, added for that session only. Codex, opencode and pi cannot receive MCP task results, so they use `cloud_agent_wait`.
2. **The main session calls `cloud_agent`** (Claude Code, Codex, opencode or pi, whichever you started) with a prompt and a short description. The call returns at once while the machine starts.
3. **A snapshot of your repo is made.** It holds the committed files plus your uncommitted edits to tracked files. It is made without touching your working tree or index.
4. **A machine is created** from the Instabox `agent-browser` image, and the GitHub token is attached to it as a proxy secret (see Secrets).
5. **The snapshot is uploaded** as a git bundle and checked out on a new branch, `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. The branch is pushed to your `origin` remote right away. If the bundle is over about 9 MB, only the commits GitHub does not already have are uploaded. If that is still too large, the start fails and asks you to push the branch first.
6. **The worker agent runs on the machine** in the repo folder. With no profile that is `claude -p`. A profile can pick another agent: `pi --mode json` (pi profiles), `omp -p --mode json` (oh-my-pi), `codex exec --json` (Codex) or `opencode run --format json` (opencode). Each is installed on the machine from a pinned version when it is not part of the image. The subagent is told to commit after each meaningful step and to push to its own branch only.
7. **After the turn, the tool pushes once more** in case the subagent forgot (and retries once if GitHub rejects it). It never commits for the subagent. If files were left uncommitted, the reply lists them.
8. **The result comes back** with the branch name and commit, and token and tool-use totals.

Fetch the work with `git fetch origin cloudy-cloud/<id>`. The repo needs a `github.com` origin, because each subagent pushes there.

### Getting the result: task mode or wait

- **Task mode.** When your Claude Code supports MCP tasks, `cloud_agent` becomes a background task. Its progress shows in `/tasks` and the result arrives on its own.
- **Otherwise,** `cloud_agent` returns an `agent_id` and the main session calls `cloud_agent_wait` to collect the result. The default wait is 600 seconds and the maximum is 1500. Each result is marked as reported, so a later wait does not repeat it.

One task is stopped after 29 minutes.

## The six tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cloud_agent` | Starts a subagent in a new machine. |
| `cloud_agent_message` | Sends a follow-up to an open, idle agent. It continues the same session of whichever agent the worker runs, on the same machine: Claude Code resumes its session, pi and oh-my-pi use their session ID, Codex runs `codex exec resume ID`, and opencode passes `--session ses_...`. It is rejected if the agent is busy or gone. |
| `cloud_agent_wait` | Waits for agents to finish their current turn and returns their results. |
| `cloud_agent_list` | Lists every agent with its status, idle minutes and progress (tool uses, tokens, elapsed time, current step). |
| `cloud_agent_stop` | Stops agents and deletes their machines. It is safe to repeat. |

An agent's status is one of `queued`, `starting`, `running`, `idle`, `failed` or `stopped`. After a turn ends, the agent is `idle` and its machine stays open for follow-ups.

## How long a machine lives

| What ends it | When |
|---|---|
| You or the main session call `cloud_agent_stop` | Immediately. |
| Idle timeout | 60 minutes after the agent went idle. |
| Session end | When you quit your main session, `cloudy-cloud` deletes every open machine. |
| Cleanup process | A separate process deletes the session's machines after the session is gone, even after a hard kill. It checks every 2 seconds. |
| Delete deadline | Instabox deletes the machine at a fixed time in any state. The default is 6 hours. Set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS` to change it, up to 24. |

> Warning: Only work that a subagent has pushed to GitHub survives if its machine is lost. The deadline cannot be extended, and the subagent is told its deadline so it can push in time.

## Starting many at once

You can start many subagents at once. `cloudy-cloud` paces the starts for Instabox's limits.

- At most 25 machines start per minute, in the order requested. Set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_STARTS_PER_MIN` to change this. A waiting subagent shows the status `queued`, for example `queued for a machine (12 ahead)`.
- If Instabox answers `rate_limited`, the start is retried after the delay Instabox gives, up to 5 tries.
- If your plan's machine limit is full (`quota_exceeded`), the subagent stays queued, retries every 60 seconds for up to 30 minutes, and then fails with Instabox's message.
- At most 24 Instabox command and file requests run at once (`CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_INSTABOX_CALLS`). Working subagents share them in turn.
- One session can start at most 200 agents (`CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_AGENTS_PER_SESSION`).

Your plan's machine limit still caps how many run at the same time. The rest wait in the queue.

## What reaches the machine

- **GitHub token:** not sent to the machine. The machine gets a placeholder named `GH_TOKEN`, and Instabox's proxy swaps in the real token for requests to `github.com` and `api.github.com`.
- **Claude credential:** sent to the machine, as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, for Claude Code workers with no profile. For a subagent on a profile, the provider key for that profile is sent instead of your Claude credential: `PARTICLE_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` or `OPENAI_API_KEY`. The `codex-chatgpt` profile sends your ChatGPT login file (`codex-auth.json`) to the machine as a file, even on Instabox.
- **MCP server tokens:** only if you added a server that needs one. The token stays in Instabox as a secret named `MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN`, and the machine sees a placeholder that Instabox replaces in request headers to the host you chose. With `mcp add --allow-literal` the real value is on the machine instead.
- **Instabox API key:** not sent to the machine. It stays in your config file and the local server.

> Warning: Each machine runs its agent with permission checks off (Codex runs with `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`), and the worker's credential is on it. A prompt injection on the machine could misuse or leak that credential. A subagent can also push to any branch the GitHub token can reach, so protect your main branch.

Output shown to you is scrubbed of known key values. See [Troubleshooting, security and FAQ](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/troubleshooting.html) for more.

## What does not happen

- Nothing is copied into your local repo. Your branch, working tree and index are not changed. You fetch the branch yourself.
- Untracked files are not sent. If a subagent needs a new file, `git add` it first (staging counts as tracked) or commit it.
- Your local MCP servers are not available on the machine, except the ones you copy with `cloudy-cloud mcp add` (remote `https` servers and `npx` or `uvx` servers). See [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).
- Your settings and agents from `~/.claude/agents` are not available on the machine.
- A subagent's own subagents run inside the same machine, not on new ones.

## Why the cloud

Subagents run on remote machines, so your laptop stays free for your own work. You can run many at once, limited by your Instabox plan and the pacing above, instead of by your computer.


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html

# Models and keys

> Choose the agent and model for a subagent (Claude Code, pi, oh-my-pi, Codex or opencode) and set up the keys each one needs.

Cloudy Cloud uses your own keys. By default each subagent runs Claude Code. You can run a subagent on another agent or model by naming a profile.

This page covers every worker agent: Claude Code (the default), pi, oh-my-pi (`omp`), Codex and opencode. Each section says which credential that agent needs. The main session, which you start with `cloudy-cloud`, `cloudy-cloud codex`, `cloudy-cloud opencode`, `cloudy-cloud pi` or `cloudy-cloud free-pi`, is covered in [Getting started](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/index.html#other-hosts).

## Bring your own keys

Each user supplies their own credentials, because Anthropic's terms require each end user to use their own.

You pay your providers directly. Cloudy Cloud does not resell model access, and this page gives no prices.

## Claude credentials

Applies to: workers that run Claude Code (no profile, or `glm`, `deepseek`, `particle`, `openrouter`) and the Claude Code main session. Workers on pi, omp, Codex or opencode profiles do not use it. Setup asks for it only if you choose claude or want Claude workers. See [Getting started](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/index.html#agent-credentials).

Claude Code subagents need one Claude credential. The setup step (`cloudy-cloud setup`) asks for it when you choose claude (or want Claude workers); it does not ask if you run only Codex, opencode or pi. Two kinds work:

- **A token from `claude setup-token`** (starts with `sk-ant-oat01-`). This uses your Claude subscription. At the Claude step, press Enter and setup runs `claude setup-token` for you, or paste a token you made yourself. Setup checks the token with one small Claude request. It is saved as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.
- **An Anthropic API key** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). Setup does not ask for it. Add the line `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...` to the env file yourself (see below). Usage is billed per use.

If both are saved, subagents use the token and not the API key.

Setup saves all keys to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env`. Setup creates the folder with mode 700 and writes the file so that only your user account can read it. The file is plain text with one `NAME=value` line per key. To use another location, set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_CONFIG`.

## Default model and choosing another

With no `profile`, a subagent runs Claude Code. To pick a Claude model, pass the optional `model` argument of `cloud_agent`, for example `haiku`.

To run a subagent on another agent or a non-Claude model, pass the `profile` argument of `cloud_agent`. Do not use `model` for non-Claude models, except as noted for `openrouter`, `codex-openrouter` and `opencode-openrouter`. You can ask in plain language, for example "use a glm subagent for this". Follow-up messages to that subagent reuse its profile.

## What has been verified

This table is the one status list. Other pages link here. "Verified live" means it ran on a real machine and the result was checked. "Partly verified" means only the named check was done. "Not verified on a real machine" means tests with a fake sandbox only. The same terms apply to [your own machine](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/self-hosted.html), where no Codex, opencode, pi or omp worker has run.

| Agent | As main session | As worker |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | Verified live | Verified live |
| pi | Partly verified: MCP connection only, no model turn | Verified live |
| oh-my-pi | Not a main session | Verified live (follow-ups by unit tests only) |
| Codex | Partly verified: it listed the six cloud tools (codex-cli 0.166.0) | Not verified on a real machine |
| opencode | Verified live | Not verified on a real machine |
| free-pi | Partly verified: `mcp list` only | Cannot be a worker |

## Worker agents at a glance

| Agent on the machine | Profiles | Credential it needs | Started as | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code (default) | none, or `glm`, `deepseek`, `particle`, `openrouter` | Claude token or API key; for the four profiles, the provider key instead | `claude -p ... --output-format stream-json` | Verified live, including GLM and DeepSeek through Particle.ai |
| pi | `pi-glm`, `pi-deepseek`, `pi-particle` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | `pi --mode json --provider worker --model ... --session ID` | Verified live (`pi-glm`) |
| oh-my-pi | `omp-glm`, `omp-deepseek`, `omp-particle` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | `omp -p --mode json --model worker/MODEL [--session ID] ...` | Verified live (`omp-glm`) |
| Codex | `codex`, `codex-chatgpt`, `codex-openrouter` | `OPENAI_API_KEY`, your ChatGPT login file, or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | `CODEX_HOME=~/codex-home codex exec [resume ID] --json --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox -c developer_instructions=... -` | Not verified on a real machine |
| opencode | `opencode-glm`, `opencode-deepseek`, `opencode-particle`, `opencode-openrouter` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | `opencode run --format json --model worker/MODEL [--session ses_...]` | Not verified on a real machine |

free-pi can be a main session but not a worker: free-pi-cli has no headless mode, and its terms forbid scripted use.

## Built-in profiles

| Profile | Provider | Model id | Key needed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `glm` | Particle.ai | `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs Claude Code on the model. |
| `deepseek` | Particle.ai | `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v41-flash-1017` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs Claude Code on the model. |
| `particle` | Particle.ai | `particle-ai/particle-1` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs Claude Code on the model. |
| `pi-glm` | Particle.ai | `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the pi coding agent, not Claude Code. |
| `pi-deepseek` | Particle.ai | `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v41-flash-1017` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the pi coding agent. |
| `pi-particle` | Particle.ai | `particle-ai/particle-1` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the pi coding agent. |
| `omp-glm` | Particle.ai | `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the oh-my-pi (`omp`) coding agent, not Claude Code. |
| `omp-deepseek` | Particle.ai | `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v41-flash-1017` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the oh-my-pi coding agent. |
| `omp-particle` | Particle.ai | `particle-ai/particle-1` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the oh-my-pi coding agent. |
| `codex` | OpenAI | Codex's own default | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | Runs the Codex CLI. See The codex profiles. |
| `codex-chatgpt` | OpenAI, through your ChatGPT plan | Codex's own default | The login file `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/codex-auth.json` | Runs the Codex CLI. |
| `codex-openrouter` | OpenRouter | None built in. You pass one. | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Runs the Codex CLI. |
| `opencode-glm` | Particle.ai | `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs opencode. See The opencode profiles. |
| `opencode-deepseek` | Particle.ai | `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v41-flash-1017` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs opencode. |
| `opencode-particle` | Particle.ai | `particle-ai/particle-1` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs opencode. |
| `opencode-openrouter` | OpenRouter | None built in. You pass one. | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Runs opencode. |
| `openrouter` | OpenRouter | None built in. You pass one. | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | Runs Claude Code. See OpenRouter. |

A profile worker receives only its own provider key. It never receives your Claude credential. The one exception to "a key" is `codex-chatgpt`, which receives your ChatGPT login file. If the key for a profile is missing, `cloud_agent` fails at once and names the key. Coordinators always run Claude Code, so a coordinator cannot use a pi, omp, Codex or opencode profile.

### The pi profiles

The `pi-*` profiles run the [pi coding agent](https://pi.dev) in the worker instead of Claude Code. They use none of your Claude allowance. Results from pi workers have no cost line. They get the MCP servers from `cloudy-cloud mcp add`, except `sse` servers, because pi has no SSE transport. See [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).

### The omp profiles

The `omp-*` profiles run [oh-my-pi](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi) (the `omp` command) in the worker instead of Claude Code. oh-my-pi is a fork of pi rewritten as a coding-first agent. It adds LSP support, persistent Python and Bun kernels, subagents and many providers. The profiles use the same three Particle.ai models as the pi profiles, and none of your Claude allowance.

Each omp worker installs the pinned oh-my-pi release v18.18.7 with the official installer, which checks the binary's SHA-256. The binary is about 243 MB and is downloaded on every omp worker, so an omp worker starts slower than a pi or Claude worker. In one live check the whole omp worker setup (clone, first push, omp install and config) took about 20 seconds from machine creation to running, against 11 seconds for a pi worker started at the same time (one run each). Results from omp workers have no cost line. A follow-up resumes the same omp session. omp workers get the servers from `cloudy-cloud mcp add`, including `sse` servers.

### The codex profiles

The `codex`, `codex-chatgpt` and `codex-openrouter` profiles run the [Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex) in the worker. Cloudy Cloud installs the pinned `@openai/codex@0.166.0` under `~/.local` and runs `codex exec --json` with `CODEX_HOME=~/codex-home`. Follow-up messages use `codex exec resume ID`. Servers from `cloudy-cloud mcp add` go into `~/codex-home/config.toml`, except `sse` servers and entries that Codex cannot read a secret from. Skipped servers are named in the reply.

Codex only speaks the Responses API, and Particle.ai does not offer it, so there is no `codex-glm`. Set up the credential for the profile you use:

**`codex` (OpenAI API key).** Create a key at [platform.openai.com/api-keys](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys). `cloudy-cloud setup --more` asks for it when codex is chosen or installed (plain setup asks when codex is chosen and no other worker credential is saved), and stores it as an Instabox secret. To do it by hand on Instabox, store it as a proxy secret limited to OpenAI, then add the name to `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROXY_SECRETS` in `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env`:

```
printf %s "$OPENAI_API_KEY" | npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY --host api.openai.com
```

- On a self-hosted machine, add the line `OPENAI_API_KEY=...` to the env file.

**`codex-chatgpt` (ChatGPT plan).** On your computer run `codex login` and choose "Sign in with ChatGPT". Then copy the login file where Cloudy Cloud reads it:

```
install -m 600 ~/.codex/auth.json ~/.config/cloudy-cloud/codex-auth.json
```

- Set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_CODEX_AUTH` to use another path. The file must have mode 600. This is the one real credential that Cloudy Cloud sends to a machine as a file, even on Instabox, because a ChatGPT login cannot be a proxy secret. Its tokens are scrubbed from replies, and the machine may refresh them. Do not pass `model` unless your plan supports it: with no model, Codex uses the default model of your plan.
- **`codex-openrouter`.** Uses `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, set up as in OpenRouter. Pass the OpenRouter model id in `model`.

> Note: Not verified on a real machine (see the status table). Resume and the ChatGPT-login error message were also recorded locally with `codex exec`.

### The opencode profiles

The `opencode-*` profiles run [opencode](https://opencode.ai) in the worker. Cloudy Cloud installs the pinned `opencode-ai@1.18.31` with npm under `~/.local` and runs `opencode run --format json --model worker/MODEL`. A follow-up passes `--session ses_...`. The configuration is `~/opencode-agent/opencode.json` (mode 600). It holds key names such as `{env:PARTICLE_API_KEY}` for the model provider — never the model key itself — plus the servers from `cloudy-cloud mcp add`; an MCP header or env value you consented to copy with `--allow-literal` is written into this file as a real value. Keys: `opencode-glm`, `opencode-deepseek` and `opencode-particle` use `PARTICLE_API_KEY`, and `opencode-openrouter` uses `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and needs `model`. Both are set up with `cloudy-cloud setup --more` (see OpenRouter for the second).

No profile uses opencode's own login, because that would copy a login to the machine.

> Note: Not verified on a real machine (see the status table).

## OpenRouter

To use OpenRouter:

1. Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys).
2. Run `cloudy-cloud setup --more` and paste it at the OpenRouter step. It is saved as `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.
3. Start a subagent with `profile: "openrouter"` (Claude Code), `"codex-openrouter"` (Codex) or `"opencode-openrouter"` (opencode), and pass the OpenRouter model id in `model`. These are the cases where `model` goes with a non-Claude model, because the profiles have no built-in model.

If you pass no model, the call fails with "needs a model". To avoid passing it every time, set a `model` for `openrouter` in `profiles.json` (below).

> Note: Signing in with OpenRouter is not available: you paste an API key. A ChatGPT sign-in works only through the `codex-chatgpt` profile (see above).

## Your own profiles

Create `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/profiles.json` (or point `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROFILES` at another file) to override a built-in profile or add one:

```
{
  "openrouter": {
    "format": "anthropic",
    "baseUrl": "https://openrouter.ai/api",
    "model": "MODEL-ID",
    "keyName": "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
  }
}
```

`format` is `anthropic` or `openai`. `keyName` must be a key in your env file whose name ends in `_API_KEY`. An optional `"harness"` is `"claude"` (the default), `"pi"`, `"omp"`, `"codex"` or `"opencode"`. It picks the agent that runs on the machine. The `codex` and `opencode` harnesses need `"format": "openai"`, and `codex` needs a provider that offers the Responses API. A `codex` profile can use `"auth": "chatgpt"` instead of `keyName`. Replace `MODEL-ID` with a model id from your provider.

Two more optional fields on any profile:

- `"fallback"`: a list of profile names. When the profile has no key, or the provider refuses a one-token check before the machine starts, the server tries these profiles in order. The result says which profile ran. A `fallback` argument on `cloud_agent` overrides it, and `"preflight": false` on the call skips the check.
- `"maxConcurrent"`: a positive whole number, the most agents this profile runs at once. Extra agents wait in the queue. `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROFILE_MAX` sets the same cap for every profile that has no `maxConcurrent`.

```
{ "my-openrouter": { "format": "anthropic", "baseUrl": "https://openrouter.ai/api", "model": "MODEL-ID", "keyName": "OPENROUTER_API_KEY", "fallback": ["glm"], "maxConcurrent": 6 } }
```

## Adding or changing keys later

- Run `cloudy-cloud setup` again (`--more` for the Particle.ai and OpenRouter steps). It shows each saved key masked and asks before replacing it. The optional steps can be skipped with Enter. `setup --more` asks for `OPENAI_API_KEY` when codex is chosen or installed; plain setup asks for it when codex is chosen and no other worker credential is saved. Setup does not set up the Codex login file: see The codex profiles.
- Or edit `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` directly. Keep the file private. To remove all saved keys, delete it.
- Restart `cloudy-cloud` afterwards. It reads keys once at start, so a running session keeps the old ones.

> Warning: A provider key is stored on each worker machine that uses that profile. A prompt-injected worker could read it. Use keys you can revoke.


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/reference.html

# Command and tool reference

> Every cloudy-cloud command, MCP tool, option and environment variable.

This page lists every `cloudy-cloud` command and flag, the six tools your session uses to run cloud agents, and the environment variables and files that change how they behave.

These commands and tools apply to every main session: Claude Code (`cloudy-cloud`), Codex (`cloudy-cloud codex`), opencode (`cloudy-cloud opencode`), pi (`cloudy-cloud pi`) and free-pi (`cloudy-cloud free-pi`). The `cloud_agent` `profile` argument picks the worker agent: Claude Code, pi, oh-my-pi, Codex or opencode. An opencode main session names the tools `cloud_cloud_agent`, `cloud_cloud_agent_wait` and so on.

## Command line

These commands run on your computer. `cloudy-cloud` checks the first argument. If it is `help`, `codex`, `opencode`, `pi`, `free-pi`, `dashboard`, `open`, `shell`, `display`, `coordinator`, `cloud`, `setup`, `--setup`, `doctor`, `protect`, `machines`, `branches` or `mcp-server`, it runs that command. `mcp ls`, `mcp add NAME`, `mcp add NAME --allow-literal`, `mcp rm NAME` and bare `mcp` (which prints that command's usage) run cloudy-cloud mcp; any other `mcp` arguments go to Claude Code. Any other arguments start a Claude Code session. One bare word that is not a command and not a Claude Code subcommand (for example `cloudy-cloud ls`) is treated as a typo and fails with "is not a command", exit status 2.

### cloudy-cloud (Claude Code as the main session)

```
cloudy-cloud [claude arguments]
```

The package installs the same command under two names, `cloudy-cloud` and `cloudycloud`; use either. Without a global install, `npx cloudycloud` runs the same command. Plain `claude` is not affected.

Starts a normal Claude Code session in the current folder. In that session the built-in `Agent` and `Workflow` tools are denied, and Claude starts subagents with the cloud tools described below. Run it from inside a git repository that has a `github.com` origin, because each cloud agent pushes its work to a branch there.

Every argument is passed to `claude` after the flags that `cloudy-cloud` adds itself (`--mcp-config`, `--settings` and `--append-system-prompt`). There are no `cloudy-cloud` flags of its own for a session.

Before it starts Claude, the command checks three things:

- It needs an Instabox API key (from the environment or the config file) and a Claude token or Anthropic API key in the config file. If one is missing, it tells you. In a terminal it offers to run `cloudy-cloud setup` now. Outside a terminal it exits with status 1.
- If the folder is not a git repository, it prints a warning that subagents cannot start.
- If the repository has no `github.com` origin, it prints a warning that subagents cannot push their work.

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud --model opus
```

It also sets `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` to 1800000 (30 minutes) unless you already set it.

### cloudy-cloud codex, opencode, pi and free-pi

```
cloudy-cloud codex [codex arguments]
cloudy-cloud opencode [opencode arguments]
cloudy-cloud pi [pi arguments]
cloudy-cloud free-pi [free-pi-cli arguments]
```

Each command starts another coding agent as your main session, with the same cloud tools. Every argument after the subcommand goes to that agent. They are subcommands, not a flag, because Claude Code already has its own `--agent` option. None of them needs a Claude token to start, and setup does not ask for one unless you choose claude. They check only that the Instabox key (or the self-hosted settings) is saved, and run from inside a git repository with a `github.com` origin like `cloudy-cloud`. Workers run Claude Code unless `cloud_agent` gets a `profile`, so when no Claude token is saved, the command prints the profile to pass (for example `codex`) and tells the agent to pass it. To install an agent first, use the command in the third column.

| Command | How the tools are added | If the agent is missing | Checked live |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cloudy-cloud codex` | Codex `-c mcp_servers.cloud.*` overrides and `developer_instructions`. `~/.codex/config.toml` is not edited. The tools keep their names. | Prints `npm install -g @openai/codex`. Then sign in with `codex login`. | Yes. With codex-cli 0.166.0, `cloudy-cloud codex exec` listed the six cloud tools. |
| `cloudy-cloud opencode` | One `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` value for this session. Your `opencode.json` is not edited. opencode's own `task` tool is denied. The tools are named `cloud_cloud_agent` and so on. | Prints `npm install -g opencode-ai`. Then sign in the way you normally do. | Yes, by the opencode build. |
| `cloudy-cloud pi` | A per-session pi extension that registers `node src/server.mjs` as an MCP server over stdio (the handlers do not run inside pi), and an appended system prompt. | Runs the pinned `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@1.5.0` with `npx`. To install it yourself: `npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`. | The MCP connection only. No model turn was run. |
| `cloudy-cloud free-pi` | Writes a `cloudy-cloud` entry (a stdio server, `node src/server.mjs`, with a 1,800 s timeout) into `~/.free-pi/agent/mcp.json` on every start. Your own `cloud` entry is not touched. A `cloudy-cloud` entry that cloudy-cloud did not write is not replaced: remove it with `free-pi-cli mcp remove cloudy-cloud`. | Runs the pinned `free-pi-cli@0.6.23` with `npx`. To install it yourself: `npm install -g free-pi-cli`. | `mcp list` only. |

The Codex, opencode and pi hosts cannot receive MCP task results, so the session starts agents and then calls `cloud_agent_wait`. free-pi is a main session only. It cannot be a worker.

### cloudy-cloud --help and --version

```
cloudy-cloud --help
cloudy-cloud --version
```

`--help` (also `-h` or `help`, when it is the only argument) prints Cloudy Cloud's own commands, then points to `claude --help` for Claude Code's options. `cloudy-cloud help <command>` and `cloudy-cloud <command> --help` print one command's help without running it. The host commands are the exception: `help codex` (or `opencode`, `pi`, `free-pi`) prints a short note, while `codex --help` starts the host launcher and passes `--help` to the agent. `--version` prints the Cloudy Cloud version. With any other arguments, everything goes to Claude Code, for example `cloudy-cloud -p "<prompt>" --allowedTools "Bash(git fetch *)"`; see [Run without the interactive UI](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/#no-interactive-ui).

### cloudy-cloud setup

```
cloudy-cloud setup [--more] [--check-only] [--provider instabox|self-hosted|microsandbox]
```

Runs the bundled `install.sh`, whatever folder you are in. `cloudy-cloud --setup` does the same, and `npx -y cloudycloud setup` runs it without installing anything first (`-y` skips npm's "Ok to proceed?" question). Setup checks your tools, offers to install the `cloudy-cloud` command (`npm install -g cloudycloud`, or a link when you run it from a git clone), copies the Cloudy Cloud skills into `~/.claude/skills`, uses the saved agent list or the agents it finds on your PATH (a fresh install picks `claude` alone when it is found; it asks which agents you run only when it finds none, and `--more` asks anyway), and asks for your Instabox key and your GitHub token, plus a Claude token only if you chose claude or want Claude workers and an OpenAI key for codex workers (`--more` offers it when codex is chosen or installed; plain setup offers it when codex is chosen and no saved credential could start a first worker — a saved Codex login file counts as one, even one a worker would later reject). Plain setup asks for the other model keys only in that same no-credential case; `--more` adds those steps and the cloud coordinators. Setup exits with status 1 when it ends without any worker credential. If an older `cloudy-cloud` global command blocks the install, setup offers to replace it (`npm rm -g cloudy-cloud`, then `npm install -g cloudycloud`). Run it again to change a key. It needs a terminal because it asks for keys. See [Getting started](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/).

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--more` | Add the optional steps: cloud coordinators, Instabox usage alert emails and the other model keys (`PARTICLE_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`). |
| `--provider instabox\|self-hosted\|microsandbox` | Choose where subagents run without being asked. `self-hosted` asks for your machine instead of an Instabox key. `microsandbox` is not configured by setup: it prints a pointer to the manual steps and exits. Any other value is refused. See [Run on your own machine](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/self-hosted.html). |
| `--check-only` | Check the tools, the saved keys and the Instabox usage alert emails (on microsandbox: the `msb` binary, the worker image, the local keys and `CLOUDY_CLOUD_EGRESS_ALLOW` — an empty exported value with none saved in the env file is reported as unset, even though a worker rejects it), then exit. Does not need a terminal and changes nothing. |

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud setup --check-only
```

### cloudy-cloud doctor

```
cloudy-cloud doctor
```

Checks the machine that subagents run on when `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROVIDER` is `self-hosted`: SSH, sleep settings on a Mac, the container runtime, disk, the worker image, slots, leftover containers and saved settings. Prints `ok`, `warn` or `fail` per check with a fix, and exits 1 if any check fails. With another provider it prints a one-line note. See [Run on your own machine](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/self-hosted.html#doctor).

### cloudy-cloud dashboard

```
cloudy-cloud dashboard [--demo] [--port N] [--no-open]
cloudy-cloud dashboard --prune
```

Starts a read-only web page on `127.0.0.1` that shows your cloud agents, coordinators and the messages between your session and them. It prints a link that contains a random token for this run, and opens it in your browser. Press Ctrl+C to stop it. See [Dashboard and app previews](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/dashboard.html).

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--demo` | Show sample data instead of your machines. Nothing in it is real. |
| `--port N` | Listen on port N, from 0 to 65535. The default is 4477. If that port is in use, the dashboard uses a free port instead. Port 0 always picks a free port. |
| `--no-open` | Only print the link. Do not open a browser. |
| `--prune` | Delete every file under the streams folder (`CLOUDY_CLOUD_STREAMS`) that is older than 30 days, then the oldest until the folder is under 1 GB, and exit. Every file in that folder counts, not only stream files. The same pruning runs once when each agent's first turn starts. |

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud dashboard --port 5000 --no-open
```

### cloudy-cloud branches

```
cloudy-cloud branches prune [--yes] [--dry-run]
```

Run it inside your repository. It lists the `cloudy-cloud/<8 hex characters>` branches on origin (and `cloudy-cloud/issue-<n>-<id>` branches, for workers started from an issue) and compares each with origin's default branch. A branch that adds no commits to the default branch (it is empty, or already merged) is marked `prune`. A branch with commits not in the default branch is marked `keep`. It never touches a branch with another name.

It is a dry run: nothing is deleted unless you pass `--yes`. `--dry-run` forces a dry run even with `--yes`.

```
cloudy-cloud branches prune
cloudy-cloud branches prune --yes
```

### cloudy-cloud open

```
cloudy-cloud open <agent-id-or-machine> <port> [--share]
cloudy-cloud open <agent-id-or-machine> <port> --unshare
```

Reaches an app, such as a dev server, that runs on a cloud agent's machine. The first argument is an agent id (the `<id>` in the branch `cloudy-cloud/<id>`, shown by `cloud_agent_list`), a machine name or a machine id (a coordinator's machine is named `coord-NAME`). It may use only letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. The machine must be running. The command needs your Instabox key.

With no flag, it opens a private tunnel from `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` on your computer to that port on the machine. It runs until you press Ctrl-C. Start the app in the background on the machine (for example `nohup npm run dev > /tmp/dev.log 2>&1 &`), because the foreground processes of a turn end with the turn. The tunnel and any shared link stop when the machine is deleted.

| Argument or flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<port>` | A port from 1 to 65535 on the machine. Write `LOCAL:REMOTE` to use a different port on your computer (not allowed with `--share` or `--unshare`). |
| `--share` | Publish a private link, with a token in the URL, instead of a tunnel. Anyone who has the link can open the app until the machine is deleted or you unshare it. It never publishes publicly. |
| `--unshare` | Remove the link for that port. Cannot be combined with `--share`. |

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud open 3f9a1c2e 5173
```

### cloudy-cloud shell

```
cloudy-cloud shell <agent-id-or-machine> [-- command [args...]]
```

Opens an interactive login shell on a cloud machine. With `-- command` it runs that command, streams its output and exits with the command's exit code. Each argument after `--` reaches the machine unchanged. Do not put secrets in the command. The first argument works as in open, and the machine must be running. Without a command it needs a terminal.

```
cloudy-cloud shell 3f9a1c2e -- uname -a
```

### cloudy-cloud display

```
cloudy-cloud display <agent-id-or-machine> [--control] [--ttl SECONDS]
cloudy-cloud display <agent-id-or-machine> --screenshot FILE
cloudy-cloud display <agent-id-or-machine> --unshare
```

Prints a link to the desktop of a `linux`, `android`, `gpu` or `macos` machine (`macos` is not verified). Only the link goes to standard output. Anyone with the link can see the screen, so do not paste it into a PR, an issue or a report. An `omarchy` machine has no display. The first desktop start on a `gpu` machine takes about 2 minutes.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| (none) | A view-only link. It stops taking new viewers after 1 hour; a viewer already connected can stay. |
| `--control` | The viewer can click and type. |
| `--ttl SECONDS` | Seconds until the link stops taking new viewers, 60 to 86400. Not combined with `--screenshot` or `--unshare`. |
| `--screenshot FILE` | Write a PNG of the screen to a new file (an existing file or symlink is refused) and print the path. |
| `--unshare` | Revoke every display link for the machine, including viewers already connected. |

### cloudy-cloud machines

```
cloudy-cloud machines [ls]
cloudy-cloud machines stop <id-or-name>
cloudy-cloud machines stop --all [--yes]
```

Lists the machines of the active provider that Cloudy Cloud made — machines labelled `purpose=cloudy-cloud`, or the older `purpose=claude-cloud` from before the rename — or deletes them. On microsandbox, listing also deletes expired microVMs as a side effect. In a terminal it prints a table with NAME, ROLE, STATE, AGE and DELETES; when piped it prints tab-separated NAME, ROLE, STATE, STARTED, DELETES and ID. It prints `No Cloudy Cloud machines running.` when there are none.

| Argument or flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ls` | List the machines (the default). |
| `stop <id-or-name>` | Delete one machine at once, without asking. The token can be a machine id, an agent id, or a machine name; a name that matches more than one machine is refused. |
| `stop --all` | Delete every machine in the list. It asks once on a terminal. |
| `--yes` | Say yes to that question; needed to delete without a terminal. |

### cloudy-cloud protect

```
cloudy-cloud protect [owner/repo] [--yes]
```

Creates a GitHub ruleset named "cloudy-cloud: protect the default branch" on the default branch: changes need a pull request (zero approvals required), force pushes and branch deletion are refused, and the ruleset has no bypass actors — nobody it covers can push around it, including you and the cloud agents, which push as you. A repo admin can still edit or disable the ruleset in the repo settings. If an equivalent ruleset or classic branch protection already covers the branch, the command says so and changes nothing. It uses your own `gh` sign-in and you must be a repo admin. Without `owner/repo` it uses the repo of the current folder. It asks for confirmation first and changes nothing without a yes. On a private repo whose GitHub plan has no rulesets it explains the options (upgrade, make the repo public, or classic branch protection).

| Argument or flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `owner/repo` | The repo to protect. Default: the repo of the current folder. |
| `--yes` | Do not ask first; you are saying yes to the change shown. |

### cloudy-cloud coordinator

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator image [--save]
cloudy-cloud coordinator start NAME --repo URL [--branch B] [--task TEXT | --task-file PATH] [--max-hours N] [--model NAME] [--env FILE]... [--json]
cloudy-cloud coordinator login NAME [--code CODE]
cloudy-cloud coordinator attach NAME
cloudy-cloud coordinator ls
cloudy-cloud coordinator status NAME [--json]
cloudy-cloud coordinator stop NAME
cloudy-cloud coordinator finish [--force]
```

Manages cloud coordinators: long-lived Claude Code sessions that run on their own Instabox machines and start workers there. All subcommands except `finish` need your Instabox key. With any other first argument, or none, the command prints this usage line. See [Coordinators and fleets](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/fleets.html) for when to use them.

#### coordinator image

Builds the machine image that coordinators start from. It is a one-time step. It creates an image machine (or reuses one you already started), installs cloudy-cloud on it, removes `~/.claude/.credentials.json` on the machine — the image never holds a Claude sign-in, because each coordinator signs in for itself when it starts — then saves a snapshot, stores its id as `CLOUDY_CLOUD_COORDINATOR_SNAPSHOT` in the config file, and deletes the image machine. `--save` does the same wipe-and-save on an image machine that is still running. The server deletes an unsaved image machine after 2 hours. Only one image machine can exist at a time.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--save` | Save the image machine as a snapshot and delete the machine. |

#### coordinator start

Starts a coordinator named NAME on a new machine from the saved image. It sends this copy of cloudy-cloud (the checkout — a bundle of its committed state plus tracked uncommitted edits, leaving out files named like credentials, untracked files and staged additions — or the npm package's files), writes the coordinator's key file (mode 600), clones your repository to `~/repo`, and starts Claude Code in a `tmux` session called `claude` through a launcher (`~/.config/cloudy-cloud/launch.sh`) that runs `claude auth login` while the coordinator is not signed in, then execs the session with Remote Control under the name NAME. A fresh coordinator waits at the sign-in until you finish it with `coordinator login NAME` — waiting for sign-in is a normal state and the machine is never deleted for it; on a terminal `start` attaches you to that pane so you sign in there. The coordinator never pauses. The server deletes its machine after `--max-hours`. Once signed in you can reach it from claude.ai/code or the Claude app (pick the session named NAME) or from a terminal with `coordinator attach`. The coordinator's Claude runs with permission checks off, like a worker, and the machine is set up so the bypass-mode confirmation and the folder-trust dialog never appear. If one still waits on a prompt, `coordinator ls` and `coordinator status` show it, and you attach and answer it. The first time, attach once and accept any Remote Control prompt.

| Argument or flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `NAME` | required | Lowercase letters, digits and `-`, up to 40 characters, starting with a letter or digit. A coordinator with the same name must not already exist. |
| `--repo URL` | required | A `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO` URL. |
| `--branch B` | the repository's default branch | Branch to clone. |
| `--task TEXT` | none | A task for the coordinator to start on. Up to 100,000 bytes. Cannot be empty. |
| `--task-file PATH` | none | Read the task from a local file instead. Same limits. |
| `--max-hours N` | 24 | Hours until the server deletes the machine. At most 24, at least 60 seconds (1/60 hour). The deadline cannot be extended. |
| `--model NAME` | Claude Code's default | Model for the coordinator's Claude Code session, such as `opus` or `claude-opus-5-5`. Rejected before any machine is created if it has characters other than letters, digits and `._:[]-`. |
| `--env FILE` | none (repeatable) | Bridge variables from a dotenv-style file to the machine; may be given several times. See Bridged env variables. |
| `--json` | off | Print one line of JSON with `name`, `machine`, `remoteControlName`, `attach` and `started` (`true`) instead of the usual text. A coordinator waiting for sign-in adds `needsLogin`, `loginUrl` (the `claude.ai`, `claude.com` or `platform.claude.com` URL the pane shows — never any other pane text) and `next`. |

About 5 seconds after starting the session, the command reads its screen. If it shows a spend or usage limit or an invalid key, the command deletes the machine and fails with that line. If it waits on a trust, MCP approval or Remote Control prompt, the machine stays and the output (and `waiting` in `--json`) says to run `coordinator attach NAME` and accept it. A coordinator waiting at `claude auth login` is a normal state: the machine stays, the output says to run `coordinator login NAME`, and once you sign in (in the attached pane, or in your browser plus `--code`) the session starts. The session runs with `--strict-mcp-config` and has `cloudy-cloud` on `PATH`. If neither `--task` nor `--task-file` is given, the coordinator starts without a task. The command fails with a message if no coordinator image has been saved. A coordinator always runs Claude Code.

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator start docs-fleet --repo https://github.com/OWNER/REPO --task-file task.md --max-hours 8
```

#### cloudy-cloud cloud

`cloudy-cloud cloud [--name N] [--branch B] [--max-hours H] [--model M] [--env FILE]... [--no-attach] [--json]` is the one-command form of `coordinator start` plus `coordinator attach`: run inside a git clone whose origin is on github.com, it takes the repo from the origin URL, the branch from the checkout, and names the coordinator an `<owner>-<repo>-<branch>-<hash>` slug (`--name` overrides; the 7-character hash of owner/repo@branch always rides along so two different repos — or the same repo on two branches — can never collide, and a slug over 40 characters is truncated keeping the hash). If local `<branch>` has commits `origin/<branch>` does not (it is fetched first), or tracked files have uncommitted edits, it warns that the cloud clone comes from GitHub and will not have them — on a terminal it asks `Start anyway? [y/N]`; off one it refuses and names the push command. Untracked files only warn. It never pushes for you. An already-running coordinator of that name is reattached to (`Reattaching to NAME`) only when its machine is running and its `install`, `repo` and `branch` labels all match this checkout — a machine whose `install` label names a different cloudy-cloud installation, or that has no `install` label at all (made before coordinators carried one), is refused with the conflict named and `--name` or `coordinator attach` suggested. `--env` on a reattach does nothing (env files apply at start only) and says so. Otherwise it starts the coordinator exactly like `coordinator start` and, on a terminal, attaches; `--no-attach`, `--json` or a pipe prints the start output only, which includes the attach command.

#### Bridged env variables

`coordinator start --env FILE` and `cloud --env FILE` copy variables from a dotenv-style file to the machine (repeatable; the `CLOUDY_CLOUD_ENV_FILES` comma list in `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` adds more). A variable whose name is already listed in your `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROXY_SECRETS` is attached by name like any other custom proxy secret — the bridge never writes provider secrets. Any other variable needs per-repo consent (`y` for once, `a` remembered per origin in `env-consent.json`, which stores a SHA-256 of the value so a changed value asks again) and is then written `NAME='value'` into `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env.local` (mode 600, uploaded through the file route, never a command line) and sourced into the session's environment when tmux starts Claude. Names that could override the machine's own configuration or credentials (`PATH`, `HOME`, `GIT_*`, `NODE_*`, `CLOUDY_CLOUD_*`, `CLAUDE_*`, `ANTHROPIC_*`, `XDG_*`, `INSTABOX_*`, `npm_config_*`/`NPM_CONFIG_*`, `PYTHON*`, `RUBY*`, `PERL5*`, `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `_JAVA_OPTIONS`, `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` in any case, `CURL_*`, `SSL_CERT_*`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`, `EDITOR`, `VISUAL`, `PAGER`, `BROWSER`, `TERM*`, `TMPDIR` and the like) are always refused. On a provider without proxy secrets every variable needs consent. Variables cloudy-cloud already sends are always skipped. The summary names the proxied, copied and skipped variables with reasons, never values; a malformed line is reported by file and line number only, and an unterminated quote ends parsing there — nothing from that line onward is used; without a terminal unconsented variables are skipped.

A coordinator machine also runs a deadline watchdog in a detached tmux session `cc-watchdog` (script `~/watchdog.sh`, log `~/watchdog.log`), started with `CLOUDY_CLOUD_COORDINATOR=1` and `CLOUDY_CLOUD_DELETE_AT` set to the deadline the provider reported for the machine. The deadline reminder reaches the Claude session through a Claude Code command hook (`bin/deadline-hook.sh`, wired for `UserPromptSubmit` and `PostToolUse` in the launcher's `--settings`): inside the last 30 minutes it emits `additionalContext` telling the session the delete time and to commit and push to a work branch — the watchdog never types into the session. Starting 5 minutes before deletion until the last minute the watchdog saves leftover work in `~/repo` every poll: `git add -u` stages tracked edits only (untracked files are logged by name and count, never staged; files already added to the index are unstaged, logged by name and never committed — a staged credential file must not ride a WIP commit), a `WIP: automatic save before the machine is deleted` commit is made when needed (a failed commit is retried each poll and never pushed), then the current branch is pushed — done means a clean tree AND `HEAD` on `origin/<branch>` (fetched each poll; a failed fetch counts as unpushed). It never pushes to the push remote's default branch (a configured `remote.origin.pushurl` is asked with `git ls-remote --symref <pushurl> HEAD`; an unreadable remote means "protected"), to `main`, `master` or a `release*` branch, or while HEAD is detached — protected work goes to `cloudy-cloud/wip-<timestamp>` instead. It never force-pushes and never deletes anything; after a successful save it keeps polling and saves again only when something new appears, a push rejected at the branch destination is not retried there but lands on a fresh `cloudy-cloud/wip-<timestamp>`, and work still unsaved at the deadline exits non-zero. On the machine, the coordinator session may also use the built-in `Agent` tool for small tasks on its own machine; parallel or heavy work still goes to `cloud_agent`.

#### coordinator attach

Opens the coordinator's `tmux` session over SSH. On a terminal it opens the session itself. When the output is piped it prints `cloudy-cloud coordinator attach NAME` instead, and you run that in your own terminal. `coordinator start` and `coordinator status` show this same command, never the provider's own. It refuses a coordinator whose `install` label names a different cloudy-cloud installation; a coordinator with no `install` label (made before coordinators carried one) is still attached by name.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator attach docs-fleet
```

#### coordinator login

Finishes a coordinator's Claude sign-in — each coordinator signs in for itself, and a fresh one waits at `claude auth login` until this runs. Without `--code` it attaches to the `claude` pane so you sign in there; a terminal is required (off one it prints an error pointing at `--code`), and when the pane shows `Login expired` or `/login` it prints `Type /login and sign in.` first. With `--code` — the way an agent finishes a sign-in the user did in a browser — it types the code (1–512 characters of letters, digits, `#`, `_`, `-`; anything else is rejected) into the pane's sign-in prompt, presses Enter, and waits up to 60 seconds for `claude auth status` to report the sign-in. It refuses `--code` when the pane is not showing the sign-in code prompt.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator login docs-fleet
cloudy-cloud coordinator login docs-fleet --code OK-code_#9
```

#### coordinator ls

Lists your coordinators in a table with the columns NAME, STATE, STARTED (CREATED when the output is not a terminal), MACHINE and DELETES, plus a WAITING (SCREEN in a terminal) column when a screen needs a look. It reads each running coordinator's screen once: `waiting for Claude sign-in` means the pane waits at `claude auth login` (finish it with `coordinator login NAME`), `waiting on a prompt: <line>` means a prompt needs an answer, `screen not read` means the screen could not be read. It prints `No coordinators.` when there are none.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator ls
```

When the output is piped, it prints tab-separated NAME, STATE, CREATED, MACHINE, DELETES and WAITING.

#### coordinator status

Read-only. Prints the coordinator's state, `waiting for Claude sign-in` when the pane waits at the sign-in (with the sign-in URL when the pane shows one), the prompt line it is waiting on (if any, with keys removed), the Remote Control link once Remote Control is connected (with a QR code on a terminal, to scan with a phone) and the attach command — or `coordinator login NAME` while it waits for sign-in. It reads the screen once. `--json` prints `name`, `machine`, `state`, `screenRead`, `waiting`, `needsLogin`, `loginUrl`, `remoteControlUrl` and `attach` (`waiting`, `needsLogin`, `loginUrl` and `remoteControlUrl` only when set; `next` names the finish-sign-in command while it waits). `coordinator start` prints the same link, and the QR code on a terminal, when Remote Control has connected by the end of the start wait; otherwise run `coordinator status NAME` later.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator status NAME [--json]
```

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator status docs-fleet
```

#### coordinator stop

Deletes the coordinator's machine now. Its workers are deleted by the coordinator's cleanup process, or at their own deadline (6 hours by default). Anything the coordinator did not push to GitHub is lost.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator stop docs-fleet
```

#### coordinator finish

Runs on the coordinator machine, started by the coordinator itself when its work is done. It checks that the working tree in `~/repo` is clean, that the current branch and every `fleet/*` branch are pushed to their upstream, and that none of the coordinator's workers are still running. If all checks pass, it deletes its own machine. If a check fails, it lists the problems and deletes nothing. It refuses to run on a machine that is not a coordinator.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--force` | Skip the git and worker checks and delete the machine anyway. |

> Warning: `--force` can delete work that has not been pushed. Use it only when you accept losing that work.

### cloudy-cloud mcp

```
cloudy-cloud mcp add NAME [--allow-literal]
cloudy-cloud mcp ls
cloudy-cloud mcp rm NAME
```

Chooses which of your Claude Code MCP servers cloud subagents get. `add` copies one server from your Claude Code settings (local, project or user scope) to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json`, replaces a secret value with `${MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN}` and prints the `npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set ... --host ...` command that stores the value once in Instabox. `ls` lists the saved servers and the secrets they need. `rm` removes one.
